doc.title: Phil Schaap interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Running the West End and playing trumpet twice
summary: He ran the West End, played Milestones on Frank Williams's horn, and declined to fill in for Charlie Shavers.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: I didn’t own the West End.
I ran it, that’s for sure.
I did everything there except play and on March 11 of ’74 obviously I played at least one tune.
How did they get you up there?

What happened was a drunk wanted Milestones. And you know you have a lot of options when you have a drunk and one of them is see if you can probably get rid of him with sweetness rather than vinegar. I mean that was one of the great night club rules. You know like not that we had too many bouncing problems there, but the trick there is if you’ve got to put somebody out in the street bodily okay cool, you earned your pay. But if I think that’s the way he’s going out and you talk him out, that’s a twenty dollar tip which in 1974 is a hell of a lot of money, or at least it was a reasonable amount of money for a tip. And so we were of the sweetness thing. So Frank Williams comes over to me and says, “I don’t know this tune, Quinnichette’s drunk all the time, what am I going to do?” And I said, “Well I’ll play it.” Because Frank Williams had — there were two times I played at the West End and both was because of the horn. I had probably already done the other one. Somebody had tried to sell Frank Williams a Colicchio horn, which is a very rare brass instrument. And I played it because it’s like playing a Stradivarius if you’re a violinist. A Stradivarius, a Colicchio cornet, very, very — and then I got into more trumpet, and remember I had not really officially stopped thinking about playing trumpet although I wasn’t ever going to do it. And Frank Williams showed me. I go — Wynton goes heavy metal? Frank Williams’ trumpet was the lightest trumpet I ever held. I always liked it, and he says, “You could play it if you want to.” “No, no.” But that night I played Frank Williams’ trumpet and we got through it and the band got a tip if I’m not mistaken from the drunk. He did get quiet, it did work, so sweetness won that day. But then I knew I would never do that again. That was the two times I knew it was over, that was one. The more important one was Taft Jordan was one of my trumpet teachers. And he liked me a lot. And Charlie Shavers was dying of cancer and was starting to miss a lot of gigs. So Shavers called Taft to fill in for him. And Taft said, “No, but call my student.” And I said, “Mr. Shavers, it’s a real honor, but they expect to hear you, and if they get me they’re not going to be happy.” And when I put the phone down, I was still living in 1006 Fernald at Columbia, when I put the phone down I go if I really was going to do this I © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-
had to say yes regardless of consequences. So I said no, so obviously I knew what the answer was.
